summary: Describes the structure, content, construction and meaning of language tags, used to say what language an object is in. It also covers registering values for them and creating private-use extensions. It is a Best Current Practice.

eli5.summary: Language tags are short labels like name stickers saying what language something is in. This explains how to build and read them.

questions: what is the iana language subtag registry
subtitle: The rules for the short labels, like en-US or zh-Hant, that say which language a piece of content is in, and for the IANA registry behind them.

tldr.problem: Software needs a shared, stable way to say which language, script, region or dialect a document, recording or user preference uses, so that content can be selected, processed and rendered correctly.
tldr.mechanism: A language tag is a hyphen-separated sequence of subtags, each recognizable by its length and position, drawn from an IANA Language Subtag Registry. The RFC defines the syntax, the registry format, the registration process, the extension and private-use mechanisms and rules for choosing and canonicalizing tags.
tldr.outcome: Registered tags never become invalid and never narrow in meaning, so old content stays correctly labeled. RFC 5646 replaced RFC 4646 and, with RFC 4647, makes up BCP 47.

today: RFC 5646 is a Best Current Practice published in September 2009. It obsoletes RFC 4646, and the unit metadata lists no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it. Together with RFC 4647 it makes up BCP 47.

sections.title: Why Language Tags Exist
sections.content:
The language of an information item, or a user's language preferences, often has to be known so that the right processing can be applied. A web browser can use the preferences to select pages, and language information can pick tools such as dictionaries, or drive spell-checking, computer-synthesized speech, Braille transcription or high-quality print rendering. One way to indicate the language is to label the content with an identifier, a language tag. Tags can also describe finer attributes such as dialect, writing system or orthography.

The document specifies the identifier mechanism, a registration function for the values used to build tags, and a mechanism for private use values and future extensions. It replaces RFC 4646, which obsoleted RFC 3066, which replaced RFC 1766. In combination with RFC 4647 it makes up BCP 47. Tags identify spoken, written, signed or otherwise signaled languages, including constructed and artificial ones, but not programming languages.
sections.eli5: Computers need to know what language something is in so they can pick the right dictionary, voice or page. A short label does the job.

sections.title: The Syntax of a Tag
sections.content:
A tag is a sequence of one or more subtags, each made of letters and digits and separated by hyphens. Each subtag type has its own length and content rules, so its type can be recognized without a copy of the registry. In order, a normal tag is: a language subtag, an optional script, an optional region, any number of variants, any number of extensions, and an optional private-use sequence. The RFC defines this in ABNF and gives the example en-Latn-GB-boont-r-extended-sequence-x-private as a valid shape.

All subtags are at most eight characters long, and whitespace is not permitted. Tags are always case-insensitive: mn-Cyrl-MN and MN-cYRL-mn mean the same thing, Mongolian in the Cyrillic script as used in Mongolia. For consistency the registry's form is RECOMMENDED: two-letter region subtags in uppercase, four-letter script subtags in titlecase and everything else in lowercase. Implementers SHOULD use a locale-neutral casing operation, because uppercasing in under Turkish rules would produce an illegal non-ASCII character.

Two further kinds of tag exist. A tag may be entirely private use, starting with x. And a fixed list of grandfathered tags registered under RFC 3066, such as i-klingon, art-lojban and zh-min-nan, remains valid. That list can never change.
sections.eli5: A tag is a row of small word-pieces joined by hyphens. Each piece has a special size and place, so a computer can tell what kind of piece it is even if it has never seen the word.

sections.title: The Kinds of Subtag
sections.content:
The primary language subtag comes first and cannot be omitted, apart from tags that start with x or i. Two-letter ones come from ISO 639-1, three-letter ones from other parts of ISO 639, and four-letter ones are reserved for possible future standardization. Subtags from qaa through qtz are reserved for private use. When a language has a two-letter code, only that code is in the registry. If ISO 639-1 later adds a two-letter code for a language already in ISO 639-2 or ISO 639-3, the new code MUST NOT be registered, so existing tags such as haw stay stable.

Extended language subtags are three-letter subtags used with a prefix, for example zh-cmn, for compatibility with older practice. The second and third extlang positions are permanently reserved, so tags that use them are, and will remain, invalid. A script subtag has four letters (ISO 15924) and is placed after the language. A region subtag is two letters (ISO 3166-1) or three digits (UN M.49), as in de-AT or es-419. A tag has at most one script and at most one region.

Variant subtags mark registered dialects or orthographies, such as nedis in sl-nedis or 1996 in de-CH-1996. A variant starting with a letter must be at least five characters long, one starting with a digit at least four, and the same variant MUST NOT appear twice. Extension subtags follow a single-character singleton other than x. Each singleton appears at most once and must be followed by at least one subtag of two to eight characters. Private use subtags follow x and mean only what the parties privately agree. For example, scholars might use el-x-koine and el-x-attic for styles of medieval Greek.

The RFC defines two conformance classes. A tag is well-formed if it matches the ABNF. It is valid if it is well-formed, every language, extlang, script, region and variant subtag appears in the registry (or it is a grandfathered tag), and there are no duplicate variants or singletons.
sections.eli5: The pieces come in a set order: the language, then maybe the writing style, then maybe the country, then special extras. Private pieces are secret handshakes that only your friends understand.

sections.title: The IANA Language Subtag Registry
sections.content:
The registry is a machine-readable UTF-8 text file made of records in a format based on record-jar, separated by lines containing only %%. The first record is File-Date, which identifies the version. Other records describe a subtag or a whole tag, and their Type is one of language, extlang, script, region, variant, grandfathered or redundant. A redundant tag is a former whole-tag registration, such as zh-Hant, that can now be built from registered subtags.

Every record has a type, a Subtag or Tag, a Description and an Added date. Optional fields include Deprecated, Preferred-Value, Prefix, Suppress-Script, Macrolanguage, Scope and Comments. A deprecated subtag stays valid, but validating processors SHOULD NOT generate it. A Preferred-Value names the modern replacement: i-klingon maps to tlh, and region ZR (Zaire) maps to CD. Prefix guides where a variant or extlang makes sense, and Suppress-Script names a script that adds no information for that language, such as Latn for English. Scope marks macrolanguages, collections and special codes.

Stability is the central rule. The Type, Subtag, Tag and Added values MUST NOT change, and a tag valid today stays valid. A withdrawn code remains valid in tags and gets a Deprecated date. The meaning of a subtag may be broadened but MUST NOT be narrowed. The set of redundant and grandfathered entries is now permanent: no new entries may be added and none removed.
sections.eli5: The registry is the official dictionary of allowed word-pieces. Once a word is in the dictionary it is never taken out, and its meaning never gets smaller, so old labels keep working.

sections.title: Registering Subtags and Extensions
sections.content:
The Language Subtag Reviewer, appointed by the IESG, moderates the ietf-languages mailing list and is the only person allowed to ask IANA to change the registry. Registration starts with a form that gives the requested record, its intended meaning and a reference to a published description of the language. It is sent to the list and receives a two-week review period. After that the reviewer must accept the request, reject it citing the rules, or extend the review by another two weeks. Decisions can be appealed to the IESG.

Only language and variant subtags can be registered independently. A new primary language needs an attempt at registration with ISO 639 first, and the RFC says it is very unlikely any will be added. Variants such as rozaj (the Resian dialect of Slovenian) are encouraged to carry a Prefix. A variant registered without a Prefix, such as fonipa for the International Phonetic Alphabet, can never gain one, because that would narrow its scope. Registrations are permanent: once registered, subtags are never removed.

Extensions work differently. Single-character subtags are assigned by IANA under the IETF Review policy, which requires an RFC. That RFC must name the maintaining authority and meet requirements: follow the tag rules, define a canonical form, be freely available, stable and versioned, and include the registration form. The Extensions Registry can hold at most 35 records.
sections.eli5: If you want a new word-piece, you fill in a form and a reviewer lets people comment for two weeks. After that it is added forever, so everybody has to be careful.

sections.title: Choosing the Right Tag
sections.content:
The guiding principle is to tag content wisely. Interoperability is best when the same tag is used consistently for the same language, and users are strongly RECOMMENDED not to define their own rules for tag choice. A subtag SHOULD be used only when it adds useful distinguishing information.

  • Be as precise as needed but no more. de may suffice for a German email, while de-CH-1996 is probably too precise. Swiss German is gsw-CH, not de-CH, which is German as used in Switzerland.
  • Omit a script subtag unless it adds information, following Suppress-Script. Spoken audio should not carry a script subtag, so a movie's Uzbek subtitles might be uz-Arab while the audio is just uz.
  • Prefer the Preferred-Value, so use jbo rather than art-lojban.
  • Prefer individual languages to collections. A collection such as gem (Germanic languages) will usually not match the tags for English or German.
  • Use und (undetermined), mul (multiple) and zxx (non-linguistic) sparingly, and do not use mis at all.
  • Use variants sparingly and in Prefix order, as in en-scotland-fonipa and sl-IT-rozaj-biske-1994.

For macrolanguages, the more specific encompassed language subtag SHOULD be used, for example crk for Plains Cree rather than cr. For Chinese, Mandarin should be tagged cmn in preference to zh, although zh-cmn is allowed for compatibility. A tag's meaning does not depend on context, and sharing a prefix does not guarantee mutual intelligibility. The tags az-Latn and az-Cyrl share the prefix az yet may be read by different people. A valid tag can also be useless: ar-Cyrl-CO is valid but unlikely to describe real content.
sections.eli5: Use as many details as you need and no more. 'English' is usually enough, and adding a country is only worth it when the country matters.

sections.title: Canonical Form and Length Limits
sections.content:
Tags SHOULD always be created in canonical form. To get there, extension sequences are first ordered by singleton in ASCII order. Redundant or grandfathered tags are replaced by their Preferred-Value, such as no-nyn becoming nn and i-klingon becoming tlh. Subtags with a Preferred-Value are then replaced, so zh-hak becomes hak. The canonical form has no extlang subtags. An alternate extlang form puts the prefix back, so hak-CN becomes zh-hak-CN. Canonicalization says nothing about letter case, and all comparisons MUST be case-insensitive.

There is no defined upper limit on tag length. A protocol that limits buffer size MUST allow tags of at least 35 characters. The figure is derived from the longest language subtag (8), a script (5), a numeric region (4) and two variants (9 each). Truncation changes meaning and SHOULD be avoided, but when needed it removes whole subtags from the right, and also drops a trailing single-character subtag. Implementations SHOULD warn the user when a tag is truncated.
sections.eli5: Canonical form is the one standard way to write a label, so two programs that mean the same thing write it the same way. Chopping a label short changes what it means.

sections.title: Security and Privacy Notes
sections.content:
Language tags used in content negotiation might be used to infer the nationality of the sender and so identify potential targets for surveillance. The RFC leaves the size of that threat to each application protocol. A tag also says nothing about the characters in the text it labels. Text marked as one language or script may still contain homographs from other scripts.

Because tags have no length limit, implementations need to guard against buffer overflow attacks, and truncation can be a result of such defenses. To limit denial-of-service risks, applications SHOULD NOT depend on the registry or the Extensions Registry always being accessible. The registry is not suited to frequent or real-time retrieval of its full contents, and implementers considering automatic updates are advised to distribute only suitably encoded differences from their own infrastructure, not from IANA. A local copy can be checked cheaply by comparing its File-Date, or by using a conditional GET.
sections.eli5: A language label can hint at where you are from, and a very long label could confuse a careless program. Good programs are careful with both.
